nameStory: Agueweed gets its name from its traditional use in treating "ague," an old-fashioned word for fever and chills, especially those associated with malaria. Native Americans and early settlers brewed teas from this small gentian to help break fevers. The intense bitterness of gentian plants was thought to be a sign of their medicinal power.
description: Agueweed is a delicate annual wildflower that stands just 6-20 inches tall, looking almost fragile in late summer meadows. This small member of the gentian family produces clusters of tiny, tubular flowers that are typically pale lavender to white, each less than half an inch long. The plant has a simple, upright stem with pairs of small, oval leaves arranged opposite each other. Despite its modest size, agueweed can form small colonies in suitable habitat.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny tubular flowers, pale lavender to white, clustering at stem tips and leaf joints. Each flower has 4-5 pointed petals that form a narrow tube, and they feel papery-thin when touched gently.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, each about 1/2 to 1 inch long. They feel smooth and somewhat thick, with a slightly waxy texture and no visible teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright annual that rarely branches, giving it a simple, elegant appearance. The whole plant feels delicate and may sway gently in a breeze.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small capsules that split open to release numerous tiny, brown seeds. The dried capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken gently in late fall.

habitat: Agueweed thrives in moist, open areas like wet meadows, boggy edges, and clearings in deciduous or mixed forests. It prefers slightly acidic soils and can often be found in areas that stay damp through the growing season. Look for it in places where grasses and sedges dominate, often alongside other moisture-loving wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of opposite leaves, easily overlooked among other spring growth in wet areas.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow taller and develop their characteristic simple stems with paired leaves, but flowers typically don't appear until late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming occurs from late August through September, when the tiny pale flowers cluster at stem tips. Seeds ripen and disperse in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist briefly, but this annual plant dies completely, leaving only seeds to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Agueweed is so rare in New England that it's been documented only six times by naturalists and botanists, making each sighting a genuine treasure for wildflower enthusiasts.
confusionNotes: The tiny tubular flowers and opposite leaves help distinguish agueweed from most other small wildflowers, but it might be confused with other small gentians. Look for the 4-5 petals and the simple, unbranched growth habit to confirm identification.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this gentle wildflower with the poisonous plants sometimes called "weed" - agueweed is completely harmless and actually has a long history of medicinal use, though like all wild plants, it should never be consumed without expert guidance.
compareHints: As the only member of the dwarf gentian genus in New England, agueweed differs from its larger gentian family cousins by its much smaller size and annual growth habit. Unlike the showy, deep blue flowers of bottle gentian or fringed gentian, agueweed's blooms are tiny and pale, almost modest in comparison.
